summary: Describes version 3 of LDAP, a protocol for accessing directories based on the X.500 model without the heavy resource needs of the X.500 access protocol. It was replaced by RFCs 4510, 4511, 4512 and 4513.

plainLanguage.summary: LDAPv3 lets a program search a directory of named entries and request changes to those entries. The RFC also defines how clients and servers exchange requests, responses and authentication information.

questions: what is a distinguished name in ldap
subtitle: A directory protocol for searching and changing X.500-style entries over TCP.

tldr.problem: Applications need a simpler way to read directory data than the X.500 Directory Access Protocol. They also need a defined way to update entries and extend directory operations.
tldr.mechanism: LDAPv3 sends requests and responses in numbered messages, defines directory entries and search operations, and supports referrals, SASL authentication, UTF-8 strings and extensions.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2251 has been obsoleted by RFC 4510, RFC 4511, RFC 4512 and RFC 4513. Its IESG note discouraged update functionality until mandatory authentication was standardized.

today: RFC 2251 is a Proposed Standard, obsoleted by RFC 4510, RFC 4511, RFC 4512 and RFC 4513. It was also updated by RFC 3377 and RFC 3771.

sections.title: The Client and Server Model
sections.content:
LDAPv3 gives client applications access to directories that use the X.500 data model, without the resource demands of the X.500 Directory Access Protocol. A client sends an operation request to a server, and the server returns results or errors.

Requests and responses for several operations can be exchanged in any order. Servers may refer clients to other servers when those servers can continue an operation.
sections.plainLanguage: A client asks a directory server to perform an operation, such as a search. The server returns a result or an error, and different requests can be in progress at once.

sections.title: Entries and Directory Names
sections.content:
The directory is a tree of entries. An entry has a distinguished name (DN), made from the relative distinguished names along its path; each relative name must be unique among entries with the same parent.

Each entry contains attributes, such as a type and one or more values. The entry's object class and the directory schema govern which attributes it may contain. Servers publish schema information in subschema entries, while each server's root DSE describes server-specific capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: A directory stores entries in a tree. Each entry has a unique path name and attributes that describe it, and the schema says which attributes are allowed.

sections.title: Messages, Results and Referrals
sections.content:
Every LDAP operation is carried in an LDAPMessage envelope containing a message ID, the operation and optional controls. A response repeats the request's ID, so a client can match the two. A client must not reuse an ID while its earlier request remains outstanding.

Strings use ISO 10646 encoded as UTF-8. Results contain a result code and may include a matched name, an error message or a referral. For searches spanning directory areas, a server can return continuation references that direct the client to other servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message has an ID that connects a response to its request. A search can return entries, a final result, or directions to continue the search with another server.

sections.title: Authentication and Directory Operations
sections.content:
Bind exchanges authentication information. A client may use simple authentication or a SASL mechanism; a client that has not bound is treated as unauthenticated. Simple authentication carries a cleartext password, which the RFC says is not recommended over an open network without protection from a lower layer.

Search reads entries using a base name, scope, filter and requested attributes. Other operations modify, add, delete or rename entries, compare an attribute, abandon an outstanding request, or provide an extension point. The RFC's IESG note warns against deploying update operations until mandatory authentication is standardized.
sections.plainLanguage: LDAP can search entries and can also add, change, delete or rename them. Authentication identifies a client, but the RFC warns that its simple password method is not protected on an open connection.
